paragraphs.heading: A domain of its own
paragraphs.text: Archaea are a domain of living things. They were first filed under bacteria, with the name archaebacteria, but that way of sorting them has been dropped. Their cells have features that neither bacteria nor eukaryotes share: membranes made of ether-linked lipids, ways of living such as methanogenesis, which means making methane, and a unique structure for moving called an archaellum.

paragraphs.heading: Like bacteria, yet different
paragraphs.text: In size and shape archaea often look like bacteria, though a few stand out, such as Haloquadratum walsbyi with its flat, square cells. Even so, some of their genes and metabolic pathways sit closer to those of eukaryotes, notably the enzymes for transcription and translation. They reproduce asexually, by binary fission, by fragmentation or by budding. No known archaeon forms endospores, which sets them apart from bacteria.

paragraphs.heading: Many ways to get energy
paragraphs.text: Archaea use a wider range of energy sources than eukaryotes do, from sugars and other organic compounds to ammonia, metal ions and even hydrogen gas. The salt-tolerant halobacteria run on sunlight. Other archaea fix carbon, which is called autotrophy. Unlike cyanobacteria, though, no known archaeon does both.

paragraphs.heading: From hot springs to everywhere
paragraphs.text: The first archaea anyone observed were extremophiles, living in hot springs and salt lakes where nothing else lived, and for a long time people thought that was the only place they lived. Then PCR, a method that copies many times over the ribosomal genes in samples of water or soil, let researchers detect microbes no one had grown in a lab. Archaea turned up in almost every habitat, including soil, oceans and marshlands. They are especially numerous in the oceans, where the archaea in plankton may be among the most abundant groups of organisms on Earth. They are also part of the microbiota of all organisms, including the human gut, mouth and skin.

paragraphs.heading: What they do
paragraphs.text: Archaea fill many ecological roles, such as fixing carbon, cycling nitrogen and turning over organic compounds. As of 2024, just one species was known to be a parasite, and many are mutualists or commensals. One example is the methanogens, the methane producers living in the guts of humans and ruminants, where their huge numbers aid digestion. People use methanogens to make biogas and treat sewage, and biotechnology borrows enzymes from extremophile archaea that withstand high heat and organic solvents.

paragraphs.heading: How they were recognised
paragraphs.text: The first archaea grown in pure culture, in the 1930s and 1940s, were methane producers, and at the time they were counted as bacteria. In 1965 Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling proposed comparing gene sequences to work out how such microbes are related, and that is now the main method. In 1977 Carl Woese and George Fox used ribosomal RNA genes to set archaea apart from bacteria. Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis later proposed three domains: Eukarya, Bacteria and Archaea.

paragraphs.heading: Why the name means ancient
paragraphs.text: The word archaea comes from Ancient Greek for ancient things. The earliest known members were methanogens, and their way of living was assumed to reflect Earth's early atmosphere. As researchers studied new habitats, they found many more kinds. Today archaea are known to be a large and varied group spread widely through nature.
